title: Universal equilibrium magic in quantum many-body systems
authors: Soumyadeep Sarma, Tobias Haug, John Preskill, Wai-Keong Mok
abstract: Thermalization conventionally describes local properties of isolated many-body systems at equilibrium. Magic, or nonstabilizerness $\unicode{x2013}$ the resource enabling universal quantum computation $\unicode{x2013}$ is by contrast encoded in the global structure of the many-body wavefunction. We show that, despite its global nature, the magic of equilibrium pure states of chaotic many-body systems, including late-time evolved states and energy eigenstates, is universal: it is captured by the thermal Scrooge ensemble, the minimally informative ensemble of pure states consistent with the Gibbs state at the same effective temperature. Therefore, for systems with no conserved quantities other than the total energy, equilibrium magic is a function of temperature alone, independent of the initial state and other microscopic features of the equilibrium state. This yields concrete universal predictions for the stabilizer Rényi entropies (SREs). At infinite temperature, the SRE is set by Haar-like fluctuations of the Pauli spectrum, while at finite temperature energy conservation induces a volume-law thermodynamic correction controlled by the thermal Pauli spectrum. We support these predictions with analytical arguments and extensive numerical simulations. We further show that chaotic many-body systems at high temperatures possess long-range magic and entanglement that cannot be removed by finite-depth local quantum circuits. Our results establish magic as a thermodynamic property of chaotic many-body systems and suggest that Scrooge ensembles may provide a unified framework for quantum many-body resources.
summary: This work establishes that the quantum resource known as 'magic' in chaotic many-body systems is a thermodynamic property, depending only on temperature at equilibrium. The authors show this universal behavior is captured by the thermal Scrooge ensemble, providing concrete, temperature-dependent predictions for entanglement measures like the fSRE. This unifies quantum resource theory with statistical mechanics.
main_problem: The paper aims to establish a universal principle governing 'magic' (nonstabilizerness), a global quantum resource, in many-body systems at thermal equilibrium.
main_result: Equilibrium magic is shown to be universal, depending only on temperature for systems conserving only energy, and is captured by the thermal Scrooge ensemble.
method: The analysis uses theoretical frameworks like the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) and employs the mathematically rigorous Scrooge ensemble to calculate the filtered stabilizer Rényi entropy (fSRE).
model_or_system: The study applies to generic chaotic quantum many-body systems, analyzed using Hamiltonians with local interactions, such as the mixed-field Ising model (MFIM).
key_observables: Magic (nonstabilizerness), Filtered Stabilizer Rényi Entropy (fSRE), Pauli Spectrum $\Xi(ho)$, and the thermal Scrooge ensemble.
important_parameters: Temperature ($ eta$), system size ($N$), and the Rényi order ($\alpha$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that local observables approach the Gibbs state (ETH) and uses high-temperature expansions and approximations for the Scrooge measure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crossover of the fSRE from a 'Haar' regime at high temperatures to a 'thermal' regime governed by energy conservation, showing agreement between different state types (eigenstates vs. Scrooge).
paper_structure: The paper develops the concept of magic in equilibrium, deriving universal predictions for the SRE based on temperature. It then compares these predictions using the Scrooge ensemble against numerical results for specific models like the MFIM, concluding with robustness checks against local perturbations.
why_interesting: It provides a thermodynamic characterization of a quantum information resource (magic), linking global quantum structure to simple thermodynamic parameters like temperature, which is highly relevant for understanding thermalization and resource quantification in AMO systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the main results. (a) Pauli spectrum dis- tribution for a typical state drawn from the thermal Scrooge ensemble of a chaotic local N-qubit Hamiltonian, shown for inverse temperatures β ∈[0, 2]. At β = 0, this reduces to Haar-random states whose Pauli spectrum is close to the Gaussian distribution N(0, 2−N) [19] (black dashed line). For β = O(1), the same Scrooge description captures the Pauli spectrum, and hence the magic, of equilibrium pure states such as energy eigenstates and late-time evolved states. (b) Magic density f Mα/N versus β. For α > 2, we predict a sharp drop in the magic density, corresponding to a crossover from the “Haar” regime to the “thermal” regime...

FIG. 2. Filtered stabilizer Rényi entropy (fSRE) f Mα versus effective inverse temperature β for (a) α = 2, (b) α = 3, and (c) α = 4. We compare three classes of equilibrium pure states generated from the MFIM (8) with 10 ≤N ≤18: energy eigenstates, late-time evolved states obtained by evolving random product states to Jt = 200, and states sampled from Scrooge(σβ). As N increases, the fSREs of the eigenstates and late-time evolved states agree closely with that of Scrooge(σβ).

FIG. 3. Filtered stabilizer Rényi entropy (fSRE) f Mα versus number of qubits N at β = 0.45, for α ∈{0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4}. A vertical offset of α −1/2 is added for visualization purposes. We compare energy eigenstates of the MFIM (8), late-time evolved states obtained by evolving random product states to Jt = 200, and states sampled from Scrooge(σβ). The black dotted lines show f Mα(σβ) −log2(dα)/(α −1) for α ≥2 [Eq. (7)]. As N increases, the fSREs of the various states agree closely with f Mα(σβ).

Figure 2 shows f Mα(ψ) for realistic examples of equilib- rium pure states, such as energy eigenstates (computed using POLFED [47]) and late-time evolved states ob- tained by time-evolution of random product states, com- pared against the average magic of Scrooge(σβ). Here, β is computed from Eq. (6). The eigenstate and late-time magic agree excellently with Scrooge(σβ), even at mod- est system sizes, and show a plateau near β = 0 where f Mα ≈N [19]; for α > 2, its width shrinks with N [48]. In the SM, we show further numerical evidence of agree- ment with Scrooge(σβ) for other local Hamiltonians, sup- porting the universality of our theory. The fSRE is calculated using the approximation ζα(ψ) ≈2N(2−α)(2α −1)!! + dαζα(σβ) inspired by Eq. (13), capturing both “Haar” and “thermal” regimes. The black dashed line shows the N →∞limit of the fSRE (and also the SRE) density, estimated by extrapolating numerical results for 8 ≤N ≤320; blue and red lines mark the limiting fSRE densities of the ground state and maximally excited state, respectively.
